documents.abstract: The rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in the cyber domain has altered the conditions of cybersecurity as it has not only created unparalleled defensive potential but also increased risks to offensives. This paper explores how AI is affecting the magnitude and sophistication of cybersecurity threats, and how AI-based attack techniques are disruptive to current security models and increase the susceptibility of organizational IT systems. Using a qualitative case study, the data was gathered through cybersecurity professionals, artificial intelligence developers, and reported cyber-attacks to examine new attack vectors, such as deep fakes, automated malware, adversarial machine learning, and AI-powered social engineering. It was found that AI-enabled attacks are performed at machine speed, which enables threat actors to carry out highly coordinated, adaptable, and large-scale attacks that a conventional defense system could not detect or halt. At the same time, AI-based defensive solutions, including predictive analytics, anomaly detection, and automated response engines, exhibit the possibilities of threat mitigation before they actually happen though they are not actively used in the majority of organizations. The paper has emphasized the dual aspect of AI in cybersecurity and the urgent need by organizations to embrace AI-enhanced defenses and fortify governance structures and invest in workforce training to combat the increasing magnitude and complexity of threats. This study could be used by the policymakers, security professionals, and organizations to shape their strategies to cope with the new threat environment enforced by AI by defining major trends and gaps and providing practical recommendations.

documents.abstract: The relevance of the research topic. The modern audiovisual arts industry is under unprecedented pressure: digitalization, the availability of DAW systems and increasing competition are forcing sound engineers to work at the limits of their capabilities. In this context, the research topic is highly relevant, as it aligns with the current scientific trend towards integrating psychophysiology and ergonomics into creative professions. Whereas it was previously believed that the quality of a recording depended solely on technical skill, science now demonstrates that a sound engineer’s primary “tool” is their own perception, which requires conscious management and protection against burnout. Research into this issue not only fills a gap in contemporary audio arts pedagogy but also addresses the challenges of an industry where professional burnout is becoming the norm rather than the exception. The purpose of the article. The purpose of this article is to provide a theoretical justification for, and to introduce into teaching practice, the metaphorical concept of the “Internal Recording Studio”. This model serves as a didactic bridge between scientific psychophysiology and the professional jargon of sound engineers, helping students and professionals to understand the biological mechanisms underlying their own auditory fatigue. The methodology is based on the approach of participant observation, drawing on the authors’ professional experience spanning more than twenty years, and on the adaptation of the Yerkes-Dodson psychophysiological law to the specific nature of sound engineers’ creative tasks. To bridge the gap between scientific psychophysiology and professional jargon, the method of cross-cutting technical allegory has been applied, which translates the biological mechanisms of auditory fatigue into the understandable language of the studio signal path. The results of the study show that the introduction of the metaphorical “internal studio” model effectively helps students and professionals develop the skills to self-diagnose auditory fatigue, enabling them to perceive it as a technical malfunction requiring a break, rather than as a personal shortcoming. The practical application of this approach, combined with the Yerkes-Dodson law, debunks the toxic myth about the benefits of “cramming”, teaching people to regulate their levels of emotional stress during complex creative tasks (such as mastering a piece or finding balance). As a result, professionals begin to consciously manage their time at the controls, which, paradoxically, leads to a reduction in the overall time spent on creating a product, whilst simultaneously improving its objective quality and reliably preventing professional burnout. The scientific novelty of the research lies in the development and pedagogical justification of the didactic metaphorical model of the “inner studio”, which, for the first time, integrates the laws of the psychophysiology of auditory perception (in particular, the effects of adaptation and “clipping” of neural receptors) with the professional jargon of sound engineers, translating subjective fatigue into the language of objective technical parameters of the signal path. The practical significance of this research lies in the development of a ready-to-implement two-stage teaching tool (an introductory lecture and “subtle calibration” through professional jargon), which enables lecturers to effectively help students develop the skills to self-diagnose auditory fatigue without the need to create separate, extensive courses in psychology. Conclusions. The proposed metaphorical model of the “inner studio” effectively integrates psychophysiological knowledge about auditory fatigue into professional jargon, enabling specialists and students to recognize their own exhaustion in good time as a technical glitch requiring a break. Recognizing this approach paradoxically reduces the overall time spent on production, improves the objective quality of the final product and serves as a powerful tool for preventing professional burnout in the audiovisual industry.

Given the continuous increase in dataset sizes and the complexity of forecasting models, the trade-off between forecast accuracy and computational cost is emerging as an extremely relevant topic, especially in the context of ensemble learning for time series forecasting. To assess it, we evaluated ten base models and eight ensemble configurations across two large-scale retail datasets, considering both point and probabilistic accuracy under varying retraining frequencies. We showed that ensembles consistently improve forecasting performance, particularly in probabilistic settings. However, these gains come at a substantial computational cost, especially for larger, accuracy-driven ensembles. We found that reducing retraining frequency significantly lowers costs, with minimal impact on accuracy, particularly for point forecasts. Moreover, efficiency-driven ensembles offer a strong balance, achieving competitive accuracy with considerably lower costs compared to accuracy-optimized combinations. Most importantly, small ensembles of two or three models are often sufficient to achieve near-optimal results. These findings provide practical guidelines for deploying scalable and cost-efficient forecasting systems, supporting the broader goals of sustainable artificial intelligence in forecasting.

This study examines the relationship between the digital mode of production and the transformation of the higher education model, using the Ho Chi Minh University of Banking as an empirical case study. Based on a political economy and educational governance framework, the research demonstrates that big data and artificial intelligence are restructuring the division of labor, thereby requiring higher education institutions to shift from a closed knowledge-transmission model toward an open, co-creative digital university ecosystem. In the case of HUB, the study identifies two key pillars of transformation: the restructuring of interdisciplinary digital-oriented curricula and data-driven training governance associated with a tripartite collaboration model. The findings provide significant scientific foundations for policy formulation and contribute to the development of high-quality human resources in the digital era.

Objective This study investigated the effects of correlated color temperature (CCT) on risky decision-making in fatigued individuals and the potential neural mechanisms underlying these effects. Background Underground facilities (UGFs) are increasingly utilized as military shelters, but the environmental stressors within them can easily lead to mental fatigue among commanders. The blue component within polychromatic white light, as indexed by CCT, has been shown to enhance alertness and cognition through non-visual pathways mediated by intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs). However, it remains unclear whether CCT can benefit risky decision-making in fatigued individuals during the day. Method We examined the effects of varying CCTs (4000 K, 6500 K, 8500 K, 12,000 K) on fatigued individuals using a within-subjects design ( N = 21) and assessed subjective alertness and mood, behavioral performance in attention and risky decision-making, and event-related potentials (ERP), including feedback-related negativity (FRN) and the P300 component. Results The results showed that 12,000 K led to more favorable decisions, reflected by a lower risk ratio, more cash-outs, and higher revenue. ERP analyses revealed larger FRN and P300 amplitudes under 12,000 K, indicating that higher CCT enhanced cognitive control and promoted more conservative decision-making, enabling beneficial feedback-based decisions even under fatigue. Conclusion Blue-enriched white light improves alertness, mood, and decision-making in fatigued individuals, promoting gain-maximizing and risk-minimizing decisions. Application The current findings demonstrate that CCT may serve as a key parameter for light-based interventions aimed at alleviating fatigue in risky decision-making in UGFs.

Despite extensive research on workplace hazards and employee well-being, theoretical understanding of how organizational support moderates the health-well-being relationship remains fragmented.Existing studies predominantly apply buffering hypotheses without examining dimensional specificity or integrating competing theoretical perspectives.This study integrates Spillover Theory and Compensation Theory to develop and test a dual-process framework explaining how perceived organizational support (POS) moderates the pathways from workplace hazards through health to employee well-being.We examine whether POS operates uniformly across physical and mental health dimensions or exhibits dimension-specific patterns.Using data from the European Working Conditions Telephone Survey 2021 (N = 10,879 employees across 36 countries), we employed partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) to test a moderated mediation model.The framework examined direct and indirect effects of physical and psychosocial hazards on well-being through physical and mental health, with POS as a moderator of health-well-being relationships.The results revealed that both physical hazards and psychosocial hazards significantly reduced well-being through their respective health dimensions.Also, POS negatively moderated the physical health-well-being relationship, consistent with Spillover Theory, but positively moderated the mental health-well-being relationship, supporting Compensation Theory.This dual-theory integration advances occupational health psychology by reconciling previously contradictory findings and provides actionable guidance for evidence-based well-being interventions.

This chapter focuses on the two most seismic impacts on education within the last decade – the COVID-19 pandemic with its resultant social distancing and lockdowns and the recent emergence of ‘Generative Artificial Intelligence’. The COVID-19 pandemic changed the way in which online learning was used and impacted the experiences of many years’ worth of students’ education, social interactions, and peer-group structures. Similarly, generative AI is already changing the way in which students find information, undertake academic work, and even interact with each other and the world around them. This chapter suggests ways in which these factors have impacted (and continue to impact) self-regulated learning and the transition to university. This chapter provides some suggestions as to how the online learning space and generative AI can be used to enhance student learning and the development of self-regulatory skills.

AIM: To propose provisional, theory-informed questions for evaluating whether artificial intelligence and robotic deployments support person-centred fundamental care when current practice is depleted. DESIGN: Discursive theoretical paper. METHODS: Purposive conceptual synthesis of fundamental care scholarship, selected behavioural and developmental theories, vulnerability scholarship, and illustrative technology evidence. RESULTS: Three lenses generate provisional questions about patient-specific meaning, connections among care activities over time, and the conditions sustaining responsive care. A separate ethical argument holds that delegating activities does not discharge professional or institutional obligations to patients. Applications to adaptive monitoring, social interaction, generative dialogue, and physical-task automation distinguish what the technology can do, how care work changes, and the effects on care. Hypothetical variations distinguish failures of interpretation, follow-through, and supporting conditions and identify grounds for favourable judgements. CONCLUSION: Improvement over current practice does not establish adequate person-centred fundamental care. Replacing an activity does not establish replacement of the care relationship. The questions require participatory refinement and empirical testing. IMPLICATIONS FOR THE PROFESSION AND/OR PATIENT CARE: Nurses and leaders can use the questions to identify changes in care and work and deficits that remain, including when an imperfect deployment offers a justified improvement over feasible alternatives. IMPACT: The questions address inadequate care as an evaluation benchmark and offer patients, nurses, and decision-makers a way to evaluate technology deployment and service redesign. REPORTING METHOD: Discursive theoretical analysis; no applicable reporting checklist. PATIENT OR PUBLIC CONTRIBUTION: This study did not include patient or public involvement in its design, conduct, or reporting.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Background: Healthcare simulation is evolving rapidly, yet its role in surgical education remains uneven. During the 9th NASCE (Network of Accredited Clinical Skills Centers of Europe) conference at Orsi Academy (Ghent, Belgium), SESAM (Society in Europe for Simulation Applied to Medicine), DSSH (Dutch Society for Simulation in Healthcare), and NASCE convened a multidisciplinary roundtable, “Healthcare Simulation 2050: Building a Better Future Together”, to explore future directions, challenges, and opportunities in surgical simulation. Methods: Conference faculty submitted reflections in advance to inform the discussion. The session was audio-recorded (with consent), transcribed verbatim, and analyzed by two reviewers using rapid qualitative thematic analysis with inductive coding. Themes were derived from both pre-meeting inputs and live discussions, aiming to synthesize perspectives rather than reach formal consensus. Results: Twenty-four multidisciplinary participants contributed, including surgeons, trainees, engineers, and industry and society representatives. Many participants expressed the view that simulation should precede clinical exposure, ideally through proficiency-based progression, to enhance patient safety and standardize training. Participants identified inequities in access, limited curricular integration, and insufficient validation linking simulation to clinical outcomes. Artificial intelligence (AI)-driven coaching, adaptive learning, and global collaboration were viewed as promising but requiring stronger evidence. Human factors, mentorship, empathy, and equity, were emphasized as essential for sustainable, patient-centered implementation. Conclusions: The discussion highlights a shared vision for surgical simulation: balancing innovation with inclusivity, and technology with human mentorship. While AI and personalized learning are expected to transform training within the next decade, simulation must remain grounded in patient safety, validation, and equitable access. These perspectives reflect emerging expert opinions from a structured multidisciplinary discussion, and do not constitute a formally validated guideline or consensus statement.

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to adversarial attacks that circumvent safety alignment to elicit harmful outputs. It remains unclear how harmfulness and refusal representations evolve over the course of multi-turn attacks, and why single-turn defenses are less effective in multi-turn settings. This work investigates how the geometry and temporal dynamics of harmfulness and refusal representations evolve across multi-turn attacks. We analyzed hidden-state representations from three instruction-tuned LLMs (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-it) using three multi-turn attack frameworks (Crescendo, ActorAttack, and X-Teaming), and examined representation behavior across conversation turns, model layers, and token positions under various context configurations. Across models and frameworks, we found that (1) each attack framework traverses different geometric directions, yet each achieves comparable success in eliciting harmful outputs; (2) multi-turn harmfulness directions became increasingly linearly separable at the end-of-turn token position across turns in middle to late model layers; and (3) harmfulness representations are weakly aligned with refusal-related representations. The results indicate that multi-turn attacks do not succeed by suppressing the model's internal representation of harmfulness. Instead, harmfulness representations become increasingly separable across conversation turns, while remaining only weakly aligned with refusal-related representations. The findings are one possible explanation for why static single-turn safety probes may degrade in multi-turn settings, and suggest that robust defenses must consider temporal representation dynamics rather than identifying harmfulness with isolated or single-turn prompts.

The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in education has transformed adaptive learning by personalizing instruction, automating assessments, and enhancing student engagement. However, the ethical challenges of AI governance, including algorithmic bias, data privacy concerns, transparency gaps, and accountability issues, necessitate a structured regulatory framework. This study develops the Ethical AI Governance Framework for Adaptive Learning (EAGFAL) to address governance gaps and ensure fair, transparent, and responsible AI adoption in education. Using secondary data analysis and comparative case studies, the study examines global AI governance models, regulatory best practices, and ethical risks in AIdriven education. Findings highlight that inconsistent regulatory approaches contribute to disparities in AI deployment, with some regions favoring market-driven AI policies, while others enforce strict legal oversight. The study recommends bias mitigation strategies, explainable AI mechanisms, and robust data governance policies to ensure AI-driven education remains inclusive, ethical, and student-centered. EAGFAL offers practical policy insights for governments, educators, and AI developers, advocating for cross-sector collaboration to align AI innovation with ethical responsibility. Future research should explore long-term impacts, scalability, and evolving governance structures for ethical AI integration in education.

documents.abstract: Introduction The increasing prevalence of artificial intelligence chatbots in e-commerce raises questions about how the service quality dimensions of AI chatbots may influence consumer purchase intentions. Drawing on Expectation-Confirmation Theory, the Information Systems Success Model, and the Technology Acceptance Model, this study proposes a conceptual framework to examine these relationships. Methods Survey data were collected from 493 Chinese consumers with prior experience using AI chatbots. The study examined perceived personalization, social presence, information quality, and human-AI service continuity as possible antecedents of purchase intention. Perceived usefulness and satisfaction were treated as mediating variables. Partial least squares structural equation modeling was used for the analysis with 5,000 bootstrapped resamples. Results Perceived personalization, social presence, information quality, and human-AI service continuity were associated with perceived usefulness. Additionally, perceived personalization, information quality, and human-AI service continuity were positively associated with satisfaction. Conversely, social presence did not show a significant direct effect on satisfaction. Both perceived usefulness and satisfaction are linked to purchase intention, with satisfaction having a stronger direct connection. The mediation analysis revealed that perceived usefulness and satisfaction mediate the relationship between AI chatbot service quality and purchase intention. The only exception was the indirect effect of social presence through satisfaction, which was not statistically significant. Discussion This study seeks to contribute to understanding how the service quality of AI chatbots influences consumers’ purchase intentions through perceived usefulness and satisfaction. The results indicate that information quality is the most significant among the service quality dimensions in AI-mediated interactions. The lack of a significant direct impact of social presence on satisfaction suggests that, in utilitarian-oriented e-commerce environments, consumers are more likely to prioritize functional service features over social–emotional factors when assessing AI chatbot services. These findings may inform e-commerce practitioners seeking to improve AI-driven customer service by emphasizing information accuracy and completeness, enhancing personalization, and fostering seamless human-AI service continuity to drive purchase conversions.

This exploratory study aims to analyse the perceptions of professionals in the field of marketing and advertising regarding the risks and threats associated with the growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in the sector. Through a survey with a sample of 373 marketing, advertising, and branded content professionals in Spain, the concerns of participants were uncovered regarding the quality of AI-generated content, the potential loss of creativity and originality, the impact on job security, and the need for human oversight. While the participants appreciate the operational utility of AI, they also warn of its ethical, expressive, and strategic limitations. The findings reveal a perspective that is critical, although not technophobic, which calls for regulatory frameworks, specialised training, and responsible use. In regards to the practical implications, this study highlights the tension that accompanies automation in the creative field and underscores the importance of ethical, balanced, and human-focused use of such technology, which is the prerequisite for a responsible transition toward the use of AI in the advertising industry. Given the context, it is imperative to understand how the transformation of the industry due to the introduction of these technologies is interpreted by the professionals who experience them firsthand. This study is one of the first to evaluate the level of acceptance of AI tools among professionals in the advertising industry in Spain.

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become a game changer in the healthcare industry, with profound effects on operational effectiveness and service quality. This empirical study examines how AI adoption affects the provision of healthcare services, concentrating on two main aspects: improving operational efficiency (resource allocation, patient waiting times, administrative workflows, and cost reduction) and improving service quality (diagnostic accuracy, patient satisfaction, and care personalization). The study used a standardized survey instrument that was given to [N] administrators and healthcare workers from various healthcare facilities, utilizing a quantitative research approach. To find statistically significant correlations between AI adoption levels and key performance measures, data were analyzed using multiple regression, correlation analysis, and descriptive statistics.

documents.abstract: Advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) have occurred alongside digitization, big data, and computing power and have significantly impacted how the global labor market works. This paper examines the effects of AI applications on the labor market and the structure of the workforce. The main method of research is literature review; academic articles on the implementation of AI and its effects on the workforce are reviewed and analyzed to understand skill-biased and task-biased technological changes along with displacement, reinforcement, and productivity effects of AI. This paper finds that AI contributes to increasing the demand for highly skilled workers who would be able to complement intelligent systems while reducing the demand for simple professions and jobs that can be automated. However, the overall impact on employment is weak so far due to the offset of job losses resulting from automation by the emergence of new job positions at more productive companies using AI.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: The integration of Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) into English language instruction has emerged as an innovative approach to support meaningful learning experiences and enhance students’ writing development. This study aimed to explore the implementation of STEM-based English writing instruction and examine its contribution to students’ engagement and writing development at SMP Negeri 12 Gorontalo. Employing a descriptive qualitative design, the study involved one English teacher and twenty-six eighth-grade students. Data were collected through classroom observations, semi-structured interviews, and documentation of students’ written products. The findings revealed that STEM was implemented through a series of interconnected learning activities, including direct observation, technology-assisted learning, collaborative project construction, descriptive writing tasks, revision activities, and reflective presentations. The integration of STEM elements facilitated students’ active participation throughout the learning process and promoted behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement. Furthermore, STEM-based activities supported students’ writing development by providing authentic learning experiences that enabled them to generate ideas, organize information, expand vocabulary use, and produce contextualized descriptive texts. The findings also indicated that project-based STEM activities fostered creativity, collaboration, and problem-solving skills, which contributed positively to the quality of students’ written products. Although some students continued to experience difficulties related to grammar and language accuracy, most were able to communicate ideas effectively and produce writing that reflected their observation and project experiences. These findings suggest that STEM-based English writing instruction offers a meaningful pedagogical framework for enhancing student engagement and supporting writing development through contextual, collaborative, and project-oriented learning experiences.

This study aims to determine the influence of Occupational Health and Safety (OHS), Work Environment, and Employee Engagement on employee performance at PT. Waskita Karya (Persero) Tbk. Data collection was conducted through the distribution of questionnaires. The study employed a probability sampling technique specifically, proportionate stratified random sampling resulting in a sample of 63 employees. Data analysis utilized multiple linear regression, processed using the Statistical Product and Service Solutions (SPSS) software, version 26. The results indicate that OHS, Work Environment, and Employee Engagement simultaneously influence employee performance at PT. Waskita Karya (Persero) Tbk, with a significance level of 0.000 < α (0.05), meaning the null hypothesis (Ho) is rejected and the alternative hypothesis (Ha) is accepted. The multiple linear regression equation is Y = 22.970 + 0.152X1 + 0.275X2 + 0.200X3. OHS has a partial influence on employee performance (significance 0.041 < α (0.05)); the work environment has a partial influence on employee performance (significance 0.000 < α (0.05)); and employee engagement has a partial influence on employee performance (significance 0.014 < α (0.05).

This study examines how employees in corporate research and development (R&D) units form the intention to use ChatGPT at work, a population that remains underexplored compared with the student samples dominating prior research. Building on an extended Technology Acceptance Model, the study tests whether perceived ease of use, perceived usefulness, and awareness shape behavioural intention to use, with satisfaction and perceived intelligence positioned as dual mediators. Data from 190 R&D employees in Tangerang Regency, Indonesia, obtained through purposive sampling, were analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM). All eight hypothesised direct paths were supported: ease of use and usefulness strengthen satisfaction, awareness builds perceived intelligence, and all five predictors raise behavioural intention, with perceived usefulness as the dominant driver. Perceived intelligence and satisfaction partially transmit the effects of awareness and usefulness, respectively. The findings direct organisations to anchor workplace artificial intelligence adoption strategies in demonstrated usefulness and structured awareness-building.

documents.abstract: This study aims to examine the relationship between university students’ algorithmic content awareness and artificial intelligence literacy levels, and to reveal the interaction pattern between these two competency domains. As algorithmic systems increasingly shape how individuals access information, users’ ability to understand and critically evaluate these systems has become essential. In this context, the study highlights the role of cognitive awareness beyond mere technological exposure. The study was conducted using a correlational survey design, a quantitative research method. Data were collected from 534 students enrolled at Selçuk University through a structured questionnaire. The dataset was filtered based on missing data, straight-lining responses (longstring bias), and inconsistent response patterns in reverse-coded items. Structural Equation Modeling (SEM), mediation analysis, and canonical correlation analysis were employed in the data analysis process. The findings indicate a positive and moderate significant relationship between algorithmic awareness and artificial intelligence literacy (r = .464, p < .001). Structural model results show that algorithmic awareness significantly predicts artificial intelligence literacy (β = .47, p < .001). Canonical correlation analysis revealed a moderate level of shared variance between the two variable sets (Rc = .473; Rc² = .224). However, social media usage time did not have a significant indirect effect on artificial intelligence literacy through algorithmic awareness (ab = .025, p = .244). The results suggest that technological exposure alone is not sufficient; rather, artificial intelligence literacy develops through cognitive processes associated with critical awareness of algorithmic systems.

documents.abstract: As large language models have been increasingly applied to daily life in information seeking and decision-making, public trust in AI output has greatly improved. This brings about the worry that human critical thinking could become impaired. Using Salvi et al.'s GPT-4 conversational persuasion experiment as a start, this paper adopts a literature review method and relies on the theory of automation bias as well as cognitive laziness. This paper uses literature review as the way of research and utilizes the theories such as automation bias and cognitive laziness, etc., to explore the psychological mechanism behind the power of AI's ability to persuade others, and how it affects different people's minds. Findings indicate that the notable persuasiveness of AI stems primarily from two interrelated psychological mechanisms: cognitive laziness, which inclines individuals to forgo independent verification, and algorithm worship, which inclines individuals to delegate cognitive authority to AI systems. Both mechanisms manifest across adolescent and adult populations and may contribute to the erosion of critical thinking through prolonged AI use. The national, corporate, educational, individual levels response strategies are put forward in this paper, and the future research directions including cross-cultural comparison studies, longitudinal follow-up researches and individual-difference study plans are given out.

documents.abstract: Aim: To examine the relationship between resident physicians' Artificial Intelligence literacy levels and their anxiety towards Artificial Intelligence, and to evaluate differences according to sociodemographic variables. Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted with 296 resident physicians working at Necmettin Erbakan University Faculty of Medicine between January and February 2025. Data were collected via an online survey comprising a sociodemographic information form and questions regarding attitudes, experiences of AI, the Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale, and the Artificial Intelligence Anxiety Scale. The data were analysed using the SPSS 25.0 programme, with independent simple t-tests, one-way ANOVA, and Pearson's correlation analysis being employed. The significance level was set at p<0.05. Results: Scale scores were found to be significantly higher among those who spent more time online, those with experience with AI, and individuals interested in Artificial Intelligence. The Artificial Intelligence Anxiety Scale score was higher in women and in individuals who believed that artificial intelligence could replace them in the future. A significant negative correlation was found between the total Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale score and the usage and evaluation sub-dimension and the learning sub-dimension of the Artificial Intelligence Anxiety Scale. Conclusion: This suggests that personal experiences and educational factors influence perceptions of artificial intelligence. Integrating Artificial Intelligence knowledge and applications into medical education may enhance physicians’ awareness and attitudes.

documents.abstract: Abstract Over the past decades, self-determination theory (SDT) has been widely applied in second language (L2) motivation research. The present study employed a multilevel meta-analysis to examine the direction and magnitude of the relationship between SDT-based L2 motivation and L2 achievement. We systematically searched ten English databases and pooled the data using random-effects models. A total of 74 eligible studies involving 220 estimates were included in the analyses. The results showed that both intrinsic motivation ( r = .318, p < .001) and extrinsic motivation ( r = .166, p < .001) were significantly and positively correlated with L2 achievement. Two autonomous dimensions of extrinsic motivation—integrated regulation ( r =. 248, p < .001) and identified regulation ( r = .190, p < .001)—were positively related with L2 achievement, whereas controlled dimensions—introjected regulation ( r = .006, p = .866) and external regulation ( r = .010, p = .781)—were not. The aggregated associations between intrinsic/extrinsic motivation and L2 achievement were moderated by learning context and teaching mode. Theoretical and practical implications of this study are discussed.

As educational systems strive to move beyond "one-size-fits-all" pedagogical models, Adaptive Learning Technologies (ALTs) powered by Artificial Intelligence (AI) have emerged as a critical solution for personalization. This paper presents a systematic literature review examining the efficacy of ALTs in enhancing learner engagement, academic performance, and equity. Analyzing peer-reviewed studies published between 2019 and 2025, the review focuses on the transition from rule-based systems to advanced Machine Learning (ML) algorithms, specifically contrasting Bayesian Knowledge Tracing (BKT) with Deep Knowledge Tracing (DKT) and Transformer-based models. Key findings indicate that ALTs yield a significant positive effect on cognitive learning outcomes and bolster student motivation (Chaudhry et al., 2025; Martinez & Anderson, 2024). However, the study identifies critical barriers, including the "cold start" problem, algorithmic bias in minority representations, and the "Black Box" opacity of neural networks (Baker & Hawn, 2021; Heaven, 2024). The paper concludes that while ALTs are potent tools for democratization, their sustainable success is contingent upon the integration of Explainable AI (XAI) frameworks and robust fairness-aware algorithms (Liu et al., 2024).
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) and digitalization are rapidly transforming the planning, operation, maintenance and management of critical infrastructure. Planning, operation, maintenance and management of critical infrastructure is changing with Artificial Intelligence (AI) and digitalization. The review covers energy, transportation, water, building, and urban infrastructure sectors, focusing on predictive maintenance and forecasting, anomaly detection, adaptive control, digital twins, asset management, and resilience planning, highlighting the potential and limitations of AI and machine learning (ML) applications in these fields. AI's forecasting capabilities help with load balancing in electricity systems and the integration of renewable energy, while intelligent transportation systems enhance traffic management, safety, and infrastructure condition monitoring. AI is being used in water systems for leak detection, water quality monitoring, and drought forecasting, while in building applications, it's used for energy optimization, predictive control, and equipment fault detection. The review also explores cross cutting data quality, sensor reliability, interoperability, cybersecurity, human oversight, governance, ethics and regulatory compliance requirements. Although significant technology advancement has been realized, implementation is limited by existing legacy infrastructure, disparate data systems, limited technical capacity, funding and procurement barriers, cybersecurity, and demos from research and into large scale operating deployment. Special emphasis is placed on the concept of explainable AI, human in the loop decision making, risk based asset prioritization and ongoing model validation as ways to provide public accountability and reliability. Future directions are: climate adaptive infrastructure management, digital twins, edge computing, advanced remote sensing, continual and federated learning, dynamic network modeling, and hybrid human AI decision systems.

Purpose This study aims to understand the role of digitalization in transforming human resources (HR) training practices and employee learning perceptions. Design/methodology/approach As part of a qualitative study, we conducted 32 semi-structured interviews, which were transcribed and analyzed thematically using a manual approach. Findings The results reveal that digitalization reshapes training practices through strategic objectives while influencing learner experiences and engagement. However, its implementation is shaped by learner motivations, obstacles and organizational challenges. Research limitations/implications This study focuses only on the telecommunications industry and is limited to the Algerian context. Future research should adapt it to different sectors and countries. Originality/value By combining HR and employee perceptions in the under-researched Algerian telecommunications sector, this study offers an original empirical contribution and extends the application of the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology framework to digitalized training practices and workplace learning.
topics: Human Resource Development and Performance Evaluation

documents.abstract: This article considers how artificial intelligence technologies affect social and labor relations depending on enterprise size and assesses the regulatory gaps in the current Russian legislation. The study uses data triangulation as its methodological basis. The empirical base rests on three sources: data from the Federal Service of State Statistics and secondary data from an econometric study by HSE University (an enterprise survey, 2022-2023); a regulatory analysis of key legal documents against four operational criteria for worker protection; and a review of publications in eLIBRARY.RU and Google Scholar for 2019-2024. The results show that at enterprises using artificial intelligence staff numbers fell on average by 0.79 percentage points. The effect varies substantially by enterprise size: small enterprises recorded a drop of 1.26 percentage points, large ones a drop of 2.08 percentage points, while medium-sized enterprises showed an employment gain of 2.96 percentage points. None of the regulatory acts examined contains a specific rule on employer liability for personnel decisions taken with artificial intelligence, and the worker’s right to an explanation of an algorithmically taken decision is absent from the Russian legislation. Generative AI tools draft, translate, summarise and organise well. They fail at the points where a practising engineer must sign. Five such points recur: a table read from an image, an analogue gauge, a standard clause, a manufacturer fault code, and direct arithmetic. Peer-reviewed benchmarks in building engineering document the first and the last. Manufacturer documentation, a preprint and practitioner reports document the rest. In each case the output is fluent and unmarked. Nothing in the text signals the error. The Verification Gate is a work method for using these tools where an error costs money or safety. It has one axiom and three steps in fixed order. It places one mandatory hold point between tool output and any commitment. It adds four fixed-structure instruments, a five-level task-tagging scale, a tool-free competence test, and a five-step installation procedure. It names seven failure classes (G1–G7) and maps each to the control that catches it. It does not teach tools. It fixes the order in which the engineer and the tool work. This paper fixes the method's vocabulary, states its boundaries, and defines a pre-registered evaluation protocol. No results are reported here, and no data has been collected. The protocol names its fields, its closed lists, and the sample size it needs. Any group that meets the stated criteria and submits verification logs under those fields is a valid application. Version 1.0 will report measured results if and when such logs exist. Files: English working paper (primary) and Hebrew edition. The instruments sit in a separate record under CC BY 4.0. While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly deployed in safety-critical domains, their reliability is threatened by multimodal implicit risks. Unlike explicit threats, these hazards emerge when individually benign text and neutral visual entities logically converge to induce unsafe outputs. Current detection methods fail to address this because they overlook the underlying risk activation mechanisms that govern cross-modal risk activation, leading to single-modality shortcut learning and hallucinated rationalizations. To bridge this gap, we first construct TriggerBench, the first dataset explicitly modeling risk compositionality (5,600 instances). By formally isolating Key Elements and Trigger Elements to build counterfactual contrastive pairs, TriggerBench eliminates risk residues and forces models to perform genuine logical deduction rather than superficial pattern matching, which provides a rigorous foundation for both large-scale training and fine-grained evaluation. Building on this, we propose a Step-Supervised Structured Reasoning training framework and employ it to train ThinkingGuard, a specialized guard model. Inspired by Situation Awareness theory, we decouple implicit risk identification into progressive cognitive stages, and utilize a step-reward Monte Carlo Tree Search algorithm to explore optimal reasoning trajectories, which are then distilled into the model through Dual-Constraint Preference Alignment. Extensive experiments across both standard and implicit safety benchmarks demonstrate that ThinkingGuard achieves strong performance. Project resources are available at https://github.com/FroggyChen/ThinkingGuard.

Supervised deep learning has advanced sparse-view tomographic reconstruction. However, conventional models, which typically map filtered back-projection (FBP) images or sinograms to clean reconstructions, are brittle under distribution shifts. Because they require retraining whenever projection counts and angles, detector resolutions, or data distributions change, their deployment in real-world applications remains limited. To address this, we introduce TomoTransformer, a transformer-based architecture that treats each \textit{local} filtered projection as an individual token and predicts missing views via self-attention. Crucially, TomoTransformer operates in a \emph{back-projection space} that separates projections across spatial locations, making view interpolation geometrically well-posed and invariant to detector size. This design yields a single foundation model that can process any number of input projections, at arbitrary angular locations and detector dimensions, and query any number of target angles without retraining. Trained on a large-scale dataset spanning diverse medical CT anatomies and natural images, TomoTransformer generalizes effectively across anatomies, materials, and resolutions. Extensive evaluations on several benchmark sparse-view datasets show that TomoTransformer significantly outperforms concurrent multi-purpose models like ViewTrans and matches or exceeds strong protocol-specific baselines, while remaining fully agnostic to the number of input and target projections. Furthermore, the model demonstrates robust zero-shot generalization on real experimental nanoscale brain data collected from an X-ray synchrotron, showcasing its practical utility for real-world applications.

Background: Health workforce strain undermines care delivery worldwide, but its structure differs by country: Poland faces an absolute shortage of doctors and nurses, while China faces geographic maldistribution of an otherwise adequate physician supply. Artificial intelligence (AI) agents are increasingly proposed as a partial remedy for both. Objectives: This review compares AI agent adoption in Chinese and Polish healthcare against each country’s workforce mechanism, using the Non-adoption, Abandonment, Scale-up, Spread and Sustainability (NASSS) framework. Methods: A narrative review followed the Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles (SANRA) checklist, given a heterogeneous, fast-evolving evidence base spanning peer-reviewed studies, preprints, and institutional reports; databases and preprint servers were searched for AI agents deployed or piloted in China and Poland since 2020. Results: Chinese cases span rule-based and LLM triage systems, clinical decision-support tools, a retrieval-augmented specialty LLM for ophthalmology, an autonomous multi-agent hospital simulation, and nationwide DeepSeek-R1 primary-care deployment; Polish cases span virtual triage engines, EMR-embedded decision-support, a diagnosis-prediction model, and ambient documentation scribes. Chinese agents redistribute capacity; Polish agents relieve clinical and documentation workload. Conclusions: AI agent adoption plausibly tracks each country’s workforce mechanism, but evidence for genuine labor substitution, rather than efficiency gains, remains limited.

documents.abstract: This study examined the formation and regulation of cognitive dissonance among 30 undergraduates majoring in English, Chinese, Japanese, Thai, and Vietnamese through semi-structured interviews and grounded theory analysis. The findings identified Cognitive Dissonance as the core category, four dissonance-generating categories—Competence Development Disconnect, Ethical-Normative Conflict, Devaluation of Language Majors, and Educational Inertia—and one regulation-related category, Dissonance Regulation. A square-pyramid model was developed to explain the process from dissonance generation to regulation. The study shows that students’ GenAI use cannot be understood as simple acceptance or rejection, but as conflicts among beliefs, emotions, values, and behaviors around AI and language learning. It also raises concerns that early or excessive AI use may reduce opportunities for sustained practice and language competence development. This study extends the application of cognitive dissonance theory to AI-mediated language education and offers implications for language programs to strengthen AI literacy, ethical guidance, human–AI collaboration, and competence-oriented assessment.

Tool-using LLM agents remain vulnerable to indirect prompt injection because trusted instructions and untrusted observations share one context, allowing malicious content to steer consequential input-filtering defenses. Multi-path consensus defenses still leave a high attack success rate because they examine content or aggregated outputs rather than authorizing effects, especially for the within-tool attack, which preserves the intended tool but manipulates its arguments. Data-Flow Control such as CaMeL provides stronger guarantees, but incurs substantial time latency that limits practical deployment. We introduce ToolFence, which compiles a typed authorization blueprint before execution, enforces it through a deterministic monitor, and when the blueprint is incomplete asks a judge to grant new capabilities rather than adjudicate each concrete call. ToolFence provides two key advantages. First, its fine-grained provenance-aware authorization enables the system to distinguish user-authorized values from untrusted observations, effectively addressing the within-tool attack. Second, its deterministic fast path and capability-level runtime grants substantially reduce the frequency of expensive judge calls, improving runtime efficiency. On AgentDojo with Qwen3-max, ToolFence reduces overall ASR to near zero with only a 3.80 percentage-point clean-utility drop and practical runtime overhead.

This report presents the work of Workstream 3 of CoARA-ERIP, whose objective is the development of a comprehensive toolkit for the implementation of best practices in research assessment for data and artificial intelligence. It covers the five Workstream 3 deliverables in a single account: the toolkit for the evaluation of digital contributions to science; the digital toolkit for responsible research assessment; technology-based tools, centred on the Modular Assessment Configurator; subsystem mapping, carried by the CoARA-ERIP Observatory; and innovative tooling, where the report gives a full treatment of research objects and badging. For each deliverable it states what has been built, what has been piloted, and what remains. It records how the workstream’s understanding matured, from early proposals for AI-driven assessment models towards governed, human-reviewed tools for evidence mapping and self-evaluation. It sets out a CoARA-ERIP position on badging, in which badges are verifiable attestations of facts about a contribution that enter an evidence map, and are never counted, summed, or used as scores.

Virtual-patient models need a way to represent a person’s biological state before they can model how that state may change. Many AI-for-science models focus on molecules, cells, or a single organ, while treatment decisions are made for people who may have several conditions and many possible interventions. We used drug repurposing as a human-scale test of whether organized biological modules can help rank known drug–disease relationships.We introduce SteeraMed Bench, which compares panels drawn from a 332-module library across drug-repurposing tasks. The benchmark included 1,916 small molecules and five primary chronic-disease tasks, with an exploratory analysis across 23 disease categories. In standard cross-validation, recall@20—the fraction of known positive drug–disease pairs found among the top 20 ranked drugs—was 0.494 for the 117-module nutraceutical panel across five diseases, close to 0.524 for the full library. In the 23-category analysis, the full library ranked first in only 9 categories; the best-performing panel varied by disease: aging-hallmark panels led for type 2 diabetes and osteoporosis, food-as-medicine for depression, and nutraceutical modules for atherosclerosis/hyperlipidemia. These findings show that different biological panels carry different ranking signals within the benchmark. Performance fell when drugs with related target families were kept out of training, and was near chance when an entire disease was held out.We also tested whether a language-model-assisted agent could propose new modules for the library. Two of 14 proposals showed nominal positive gains in the second round, but neither remained significant after correction for testing seven concepts. SteeraMed Bench provides a shared way to compare and update biological representations for future virtual-patient research. It is a benchmark for representation and candidate prioritization, not a complete virtual patient or a validated drug-discovery system.

documents.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a cornerstone for improving the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs), but the need for on-policy data substantially limits training efficiency. Reusing off-policy data through importance sampling (IS) can improve efficiency but introduce considerable instability. Hence, algorithms such as PPO and GRPO widely adopt IS-ratio clipping to stabilize training. However, training stability and gradient estimate are mainly determined by the product of IS ratio and advantage. To further stabilize training, we propose ACPO, which clips the product of the IS ratio and the advantage, leading to more stable gradient estimates. We also establish a connection between ACPO and gradient clipping in policy mirror descent (PMD), which is a standard technique to stabilize optimization process, and prove the convergence of clipped-PMD under the standard RL setting. Experiments on widely used mathematical reasoning benchmarks show that ACPO consistently outperforms PPO and GRPO in both accuracy and training efficiency, delivering 4-6 percentage points gains on standard math benchmarks, with Qwen3-8B+PPO. Hence, ACPO is a practical and effective alternative to conventional IS-ratio clipping for RL post-training of LLMs.

Summary Many appeals to farmers to adopt sustainable practices are currently relying on pressure factors that may be inducing green and yet unsustainable behaviour. Different trade‐offs are involved in this transition but are normally overlooked. Take for example those sustainable practices that are intended to substitute away from synthetic fertilisers. Being a key input in the production process, promoting farmers’ transition to more sustainable fertiliser practices is challenging and uptake remains low. Recent extremely high fertiliser prices, especially due to the Russian invasion of Ukraine, and its volatility, have added considerable pressure on farmers to consider fertiliser substitutes. Furthermore, more restrictive environmental regulations, such as reductions in nitrogen allowances, have added another substantial pressure on farmers to look for alternatives. To some extent, high prices and legislation may ‘force’ farmers to increase the adoption of sustainable fertilisers. However, this increased adoption will be superficial and unsustainable if farmers are feeling pushed into these changes. We believe that farmers’ intrinsic motives (e.g. environmental concern, morale, or responsibility) to adopt sustainable fertiliser practices have not yet been engaged in adoption decisions. Therefore, we argue that as soon as synthetic fertiliser prices go down, or if environmental regulations are eased, farmers will go back to their conventional fertiliser practices. Improving farmers' intrinsic motivation could therefore provide a more sustainable approach to reducing synthetic fertiliser application than relying solely on external pressures, an aspect that has received limited attention in policy.

On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) improves large language models by letting a self-teacher with privileged information provide dense token-level supervision on the model's own trajectories. Yet existing methods typically construct the self-teacher from the current, initial, or slowly averaged policy state, leaving the quality of supervision constrained by the teacher's ability to exploit privileged information. We ask whether the model's own optimization progress can instead be recycled into a stronger self-teacher. In this paper, we introduce Bootstrapped On-Policy Self-Distillation (B-OPSD), which temporarily trains the policy ahead to obtain a future teacher, restores the student to the original policy state, and then uses the future teacher to supervise the restarted student. The future teacher improves supervision in two complementary ways, it can generate more reliable privileged trajectories and, conditioned on them, provide more informative token-level targets along the restarted student's on-policy trajectories. Experiments on mathematical reasoning with Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B show consistent improvements over standard OPSD in both settings, including gains from 27.50 to 41.30 and from 48.80 to 64.44 in the rollout-privileged setting. Our findings point to a broader principle for self-improving models that future learning progress can be distilled backward, preserving acquired knowledge while bootstrapping beyond the optimization state that produced it.

Mid-training equips pretrained large language models with specialized and reasoning capabilities, but the returns of this stage are bounded since additional serial compute yields little further downstream improvement and can even degrade some capabilities, which places a practical ceiling on how much compute mid-training absorbs. We revisit how this compute should be allocated to a single run or multiple similar optimizations. We find that branches forked from a shared checkpoint under various controlled recipe reaches measurably different regions of parameter space, and establish a form of compatible diversity that extending one run cannot supply. Therefore, we introduce Trajectory Soup, which distributes a mid-training budget over several independent branches, and consolidates strongest checkpoints selected on validation through intra- and inter-trajectory averaging into a single model. A local bias and variance analysis separates the two averaging levels, showing that inter-trajectory averaging removes residual error beyond the reach of averaging within a trajectory, while checkpoint selection carries a bias that bounds how many checkpoints are worth merging. Across model scales, learning-rate schedules, token budgets, and trajectory counts, Trajectory Soup improves aggregate downstream performance over the strongest single-trajectory average under matched budgets and keeps improving as budgets expand, with the advantage preserved after an identical post-training pipeline. These results position trajectory allocation and merging as a practical way to extend the compute-scaling frontier of mid-training beyond serial saturation.

Abstract: This study aims to map the determinants of digital culture transformation in Senior High Schools (SMA) through a Systematic Literature Review (SLR). The method applies PRISMA and PSALSAR frameworks to 17 articles (2020–2026) from Google Scholar, ScienceDirect, and Garuda. The findings identify three main factors: transformational leadership, teachers’ digital competence, and students’ autonomy support. Leadership acts as a catalyst for technology integration, teacher competence improves performance through motivation and discipline, while digital media enhances student digital literacy. The study concludes that digital culture transformation is driven more by human factors than technological infrastructure. Metode menggunakan PRISMA dan PSALSAR terhadap 17 artikel (2020–2026) dari Google Scholar, ScienceDirect, dan Garuda. Hasil menunjukkan tiga faktor utama, yaitu kepemimpinan transformasional, kompetensi digital guru, dan dukungan otonomi siswa. Kepemimpinan berperan sebagai katalis integrasi teknologi, kompetensi guru meningkatkan kinerja melalui motivasi dan disiplin, sedangkan media digital mendukung literasi siswa. Temuan menegaskan bahwa transformasi budaya digital lebih ditentukan oleh faktor manusia dibandingkan infrastruktur teknologi. User-written Triton kernels enable high-performance GPU computation within PyTorch, but their end-to-end latency can remain dominated by host-side orchestration, especially when device execution is short. Although torch.compile can generate native host wrappers for captured graphs, each invocation still passes through runtime-managed specialization lookup, guard evaluation, and preparation before reaching the wrapper. We present Trident, a compiler backend that removes this recurring overhead from the specialization cache-hit path. Trident introduces the Specialization Cache Module (SCM), which compiles guarded specialization selection, argument and execution-environment preparation, and host execution for multiple specializations into a single executable module. An invocation enters the SCM once, remains in compiled code when a specialization matches, and returns to Python only when a new specialization must be compiled. Built on Torch-MLIR, Trident lowers guards and host-side orchestration to native code while retaining calls to optimized runtime implementations of supported ATen operators. Our evalu- ation on two LLMs shows that Trident achieves up to a 1.47x speedup in model-level end-to-end latency over eager execution and up to 1.68x over torch.compile.

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT: Purpose. The Philippine Inclusive Education Act of 2022 shifted the teaching of disabled students to general education classrooms wherein collaboration between the special education (SNEd) teacher and the general education teacher shall be an ordinary condition of basic education. The benefit of international synthesis, however, is that they highlight that co-taught classrooms tend to become setups where one teacher teaches and the other teacher helps, and there is little use of small group teaching, moving the specialist to an assistant role. The current research explored that phenomenon from a practitioner's perspective was most impacted by the phenomenon. Method. The convergent mixed methods design was used and total enumeration, covering sixty (60) special education teachers in one Schools Division Office in the National Capital Region in the Philippines was employed. Validated (by 5 experts; S-CVI/Ave = 0.94) and pilot-tested (externally; α = 0.84-0.93) researcher-made instrument was used to generate quantitative data, while two focus group discussions were used to generate qualitative data, which was achieved with open-ended prompts. Weighted mean, standard deviation, Mann-Whitney U and Kruskal-Wallis H tests were used for analysis, and reflexive thematic analysis was used for the narrative strand. Findings. The one teach–one assist configuration was used Often (M = 4.18) and the three small–group –generating configurations had a composite rating of 2.49 (Rarely). The highest level of implementation was for in-lesson behaviors that a specialist engages in alone, while the lowest was for recognized instructional parity (M = 2.12) and joint planning pre-lesson (M = 2.25). Learner perceived confidence was rated Very Highly Evident (M = 3.29), engagement Highly Evident (M = 3.16), and cognitive engagement was the lowest (M = 2.95). Of all the outcome domains (implementation: H = 18.44, p < .001), only common planning time distinguished all three sections, with the threshold between "almost none" and "thirty minutes weekly". There was significant correlation between implementation and confidence (ρ = .617) and engagement (ρ = .584). Contribution. The study provides a mechanism for implementing inclusive education at the configuration level, which is not included in Philippine inclusive education research, demonstrates that the limitation of inclusive practice in an urban division is administrative, not attitudinal, and, pinpoints an intervention point that is low cost and high yield in protected weekly co-planning time. Keywords: co-teaching; inclusive education; special education teachers; small-group learning; learner engagement; Philippines

Recent approaches to reinforcement learning (RL) post-training for large language models increasingly remove the critic to reduce training instability and memory overhead. Even where a critic is trained, it is discarded once training ends, although it has learned to predict outcomes. We revisit this trend and show that a pretrained critic's ability to predict future outcomes can make it a valuable asset for efficient long-horizon reasoning. First, we find that instability in critic-based RL for long chain-of-thought reasoning is largely an optimization artifact: keeping policy updates small and low in variance restores stable convergence. Second, a well-pretrained critic estimates the posterior probability of eventual success from later trajectory states and unfinished prefixes. Its predictions provide outcome-derived, dense, per-prefix learning signals that, during policy optimization, require neither completed rollouts, step-level annotations, nor external reward labels. Building on this insight, we introduce Reward-Free Policy Optimization (RFPO), which repurposes a single calibrated, frozen critic as a rollout-level reward, a value baseline for generalized advantage estimation, and a success forecaster for unfinished prefixes. We further show that binarizing the debiased score stops the policy from exploiting the critic's length bias. Binarized, RFPO matches supervised PPO without a single label in the training loop, while cutting compute and memory overhead. This makes RFPO well suited to long-horizon reasoning tasks, where outcomes arrive late and generation dominates cost: because rollouts can be rewarded before they finish, training no longer has to pay for waiting on every trajectory to complete. Our findings challenge the prevailing critic-free paradigm and establish critic-based, reward-free optimization as a scalable and computationally efficient path for LLM post-training.

This preliminary fNIRS study examined how miners' safety psychology and self-involvement relate to safety decision-making. Both factors were associated with safe-decision rates, while their interaction affected reaction time. Hemodynamic responses in frontal and temporal regions also varied across decision stages. These findings suggest that individual and situational factors may influence mining-safety decisions, supporting training that addresses risks to miners and coworkers.

Large language model (LLM) agents reuse external memory to guide new tasks, but effective retrieval requires learning which memory sets improve execution. Such learning relies on costly outcome feedback: ordinary retrieval observes only executed sets, while evaluating alternatives requires additional rollouts. We introduce \textsc{UpliftMem}, which learns memory retrieval from set-level execution uplift relative to the same executor without memory. A theoretical analysis of how retrieval preferences restrict feedback coverage motivates targeted probing of alternative memory sets. Probe selection follows an expected value of sample information (EVSI) criterion, derived in closed form under a correlated Gaussian model, to allocate limited training rollouts according to their expected improvement in local retrieval decisions. The shared scorer is trained with a frozen executor and selects memory sets without test-time probes. Across ALFWorld, WebShop, and BigCodeBench, \textsc{UpliftMem} achieves the best success rates among evaluated baselines on the main evaluation sets. Controlled fixed-store and matched probe budget evaluations further demonstrate improved memory-use decisions and more effective use of execution feedback.

The effective use of electronic medical records (EMRs) has become increasingly vital to ensuring quality and safety in healthcare delivery in Egypt. Yet, user satisfaction and perceptions of usability often hinge on how work is structured within clinical settings. This study aimed to assess how healthcare professionals in Egypt, perceive the usability of EMR interface and how their satisfaction is shaped by the work design under the Universal Health Insurance (UHI) system. Methods An analytical cross-sectional study was conducted among 532 healthcare professionals working in UHI-affiliated primary and secondary healthcare facilities. Data was collected using a structured questionnaire that combined the Questionnaire for User Interaction Satisfaction and Short Version of the Work Design. Statistical analysis was performed using non-parametric methods in SPSS. Results Healthcare professionals reported an overall median EMR satisfaction score of 6.8. Screen design received the highest rating (median = 7.3), followed by terminology and system information and learning (both median = 7.1), while system capabilities (median = 6.6) and general impressions (median = 6.5) received lower ratings. The median overall work-design score was 3.7, with task significance and social support rated most favorably, while autonomy received relatively lower scores. A moderate positive correlation was observed between work design and EMR satisfaction (ρ = 0.48, p < 0.001). In bivariate analyses, gender and language used for EMR data entry were significantly associated with EMR satisfaction, while years of EMR experience were associated with work design perceptions. In the multivariable model, work design was the only independent predictor of overall EMR satisfaction (β = 0.47, p < 0.001). Conclusion Improving system responsiveness and addressing work-design characteristics, particularly autonomy, social support and feedback from others, may support better EMR user experiences.

This article examines current issues regarding the legal regulation of works made for hire created using generative artificial intelligence within the scientific field. The author analyzes the legal conflict between the classical institution of authorship and modern algorithmic solutions. The study provides a detailed overview of the eligibility criteria for scientific texts and evaluates the creative contribution of researchers when formulating search queries. Particular emphasis is placed on analyzing foreign judicial practice and the provisions of the draft Federal Law on the state regulation of artificial intelligence dated March 2026. As a result of the research, proposals are formulated for introducing a legal presumption of authorship for neural network operators. The author justifies the need for adopting local regulations within research and educational organizations to minimize the risks of hidden plagiarism and ensure the correct transfer of exclusive rights to the employer.

Interactive agent benchmarks and multi-turn reinforcement learning increasingly place a second language model in the role of the user. This simulated user controls what information the agent receives and when, yet current benchmarks score only the agent and do not directly measure whether the user correctly executed its assigned role. We introduce UserProxyBench, an evaluation layer over the tau-bench family, and the User Fidelity Score (UFS), which measures adherence to the benchmark's private user instructions using task-grounded rubric criteria scored independently of agent success. Holding the agent fixed at GPT-5.5 and varying only the user proxy across 375 enterprise tasks changes mean task reward by 15.2 points, while 24.4% of successful episodes contain a user-specification violation. The dominant failure is premature disclosure: users provide information before it is requested. This behavior has little effect on task reward, yet among successful episodes it causes the agent to make 1.06 fewer tool calls on average, changing the interaction being evaluated while preserving the reward. Finally, across seven proxies we identify an empirical cost-fidelity frontier, enabling practitioners to select the least expensive simulator that satisfies a required fidelity level.

documents.abstract: This exploratory study examines graduate students’ perceptions of generative AI use in coursework and evaluates the feasibility of using large language models (LLMs) to support thematic coding of brief open-ended responses. Students ( n = 20) enrolled in a systems analysis and design course completed a post-course survey consisting of Likert-scale items and eight open-ended questions, six retrospective and two prospective or hypothetical. Quantitative responses were summarized descriptively, while qualitative responses were independently coded by two human researchers and two LLMs (GPT-4o and Claude 3.7 Sonnet) using a shared, human-developed codebook. Inter-rater reliability was assessed using Cohen’s and Fleiss’ kappa. Students reported high levels of engagement, motivation, perceived learning support, and perceived efficiency when using course-specific LLM applications; however, the study did not assess objective learning outcomes. Human-human agreement ranged from moderate to almost perfect (κ = 0.52–0.84), whereas average human-LLM agreement was lower and more variable (κ = 0.36–0.62). Claude aligned more closely with the human coders than GPT-4o across all eight questions when the two human-model kappas were averaged. Agreement was highest for concrete, task-focused prompts and lower for several reflective and prospective prompts, where the LLMs missed human-identified themes, fragmented broad themes into narrower subcodes, or assigned substantive meaning to non-responses. Hybrid intelligent feedback is used as a retrospective sensitizing framework rather than as a prospectively operationalized intervention. The findings support a bounded role for LLMs in qualitative educational research: models can assist with screening, discrepancy detection, and code suggestions, but human researchers remain necessary for contextual interpretation, validation, and adjudication.

documents.abstract: Chinese Semantic Error Correction (CSEC) targets semantic errors in Chinese text, which are typically more subtle and complex than spelling and grammatical errors but remain relatively underexplored. Existing LLM-based approaches face two recurring obstacles in this task: over-correction, and unclear interaction between Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning and self-consistency decoding, such that the benefits brought by CoT cannot be reliably transferred to final corrections. We propose Vote-guided Advantage Allocation for CSEC (VAA-CSEC), a multi-stage framework that combines CoT distillation, Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), Reinforcement Learning (RL) and self-consistency decoding. During RL, we design a task-specific reward function that directly aligned with the minimal-editing principle of CSEC. We further introduce Group-Level Relative Policy Optimization (GLPO), which reallocates GRPO advantages according to the margin between individual rollout rewards and the vote-aggregated group reward, aligning the RL training objective with the self-consistency objective used at inference time. Experiments on CSED-C and NaSGEC-Exam show that VAA-CSEC outperforms all LLM-based baselines on CSED-C with an F0.5 of 47.72%, achieves the highest recall of 42.15% among all methods, and establishes a new state of the art of 41.55% F0.5 on NaSGEC-Exam.

The application of artificial intelligence (AI) in ophthalmology has emerged as a promising strategy for the early diagnosis and population screening of visual diseases, mitigating the shortage of specialists and optimizing the management of health resources. The present study aims to analyze the clinical efficacy, robustness, and generalization capacity of AI algorithms applied to the screening and diagnostic support of ophthalmological pathologies. For this purpose, an integrative literature review was conducted through searches in the Google Scholar, PubMed, ResearchGate, and CAPES Periodicals Portal databases, culminating in the selection and analysis of ten studies published between 2018 and 2025. The synthesis of evidence demonstrated that deep learning models focused on the analysis of fundus images present high rates of sensitivity and specificity, especially in the detection of diabetic retinopathy, retinopathy of prematurity, glaucoma, and age-related macular degeneration. Furthermore, it was found that the integration of these technologies significantly expands clinical screening capacity. However, the performance of these algorithms can undergo significant variations when faced with distinct populations or different capture equipment, a technical challenge known as domain shift. Therefore, it is inferred that the safe clinical implementation of AI requires rigorous multicenter external validations and the development of clear ethical-regulatory guidelines, acting as a complement to medical judgment and democratizing access to visual care.
